newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bavaria's Stoiber-delay best if EMU targets missed.
newsitem.headline: Bavaria's Stoiber-delay best if EMU targets missed.

text.p: Bavarian Premier Edmund Stoiber was quoted on Thursday as saying it would be best to delay European economic and monetary union (EMU) if France or Germany did not respect criteria in the Maastricht treaty "to the letter".
"If France or Germany do not respect the criteria to the letter we will find another alternative," Stoiber said in an interview with financial daily La Tribune.

"I can easily imagine that the best solution is to give ourselves two extra years, until 1999, to meet the criteria and then reduce the intermediate phase," Stoiber, a member of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union party, said.
European exchange rate parities are due to be fixed on January 1, 1999, with euro bills and coins coming into circulation in 2002.

Stoiber said European countries did not need three years to put the euro into operation and that by fixing exchange rates on January 1, 2001, instead of in 1999 as planned, Europe could still introduce the new currency on time in 2002.
His comments echoed similar statements quoted on Wednesday by Dutch newspaper Algemeen Dagblad.

A spokesman for Stoiber said later on Wednesday no plan to delay EMU existed and the comments were simply "hypothetical reflections" on what should happen if countries failed to fulfil the entry criteria set by the Maastricht treaty.

Stoiber told La Tribune that lasting respect for the Maastricht treaty criteria was "primordial" and the recognition of their importance was what had led to the signing of a so-called stability pact to impose fines on countries in EMU whose deficits climbed above three percent of gross domestic product from 1998.
"So there is no reason to be more flexible in 1997," he told the paper.
"You can say the criteria are key, since they are the only guarantors of economic policy convergence. They are, therefore, clearly more important than the calendar."
He said he thought it would be impossible for the euro to start if Germany did not respect the treaty criteria to the letter.
